{{nihongo|'''Kashima Shrine'''|鹿島神宮|Kashima Jingū}} is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|qid=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine|1=Shinto shrine}} located in {{ill|Kashima, Ibaraki|en|Kashima, Ibaraki|qid=Q467471|lt=Kashima, Ibaraki|1=Kashima, Ibaraki}} in the northern {{ill|Kantō region|en|Kantō region|qid=Q132480|lt=Kantō region|1=Kantō region}} of Japan. It is dedicated to {{nihongo|[[Takemikazuchi]]-no-Ōkami|武甕槌大神|}}, one of the [[:en:Patron deities|Patron deities]] of {{ill|Martial arts|en|Martial arts|qid=Q11417|lt=Martial arts|1=Martial arts}}. Various [[:en:Dōjō|Dōjō]] of ''{{ill|Kenjutsu|en|Kenjutsu|qid=Q249608|lt=Kenjutsu|1=Kenjutsu}}'' and ''[[:en:Kendō|Kendō]]'' often display a [[:en:Kakejiku|hanging scroll]] emblazoned with the name "Takemikazuchi-no-Ōkami". Prior to World War II, the shrine was Ranked as one of the three most important imperial shrines {{nihongo|{{ill|List of Jingū|en|List of Jingū|qid=Q120680118|lt=Jingū|1=List of Jingū}}|神宮|}} in the Shinto hierarchy, along with [[Ise Grand Shrine]] (伊勢神宮 ''Ise Jingū'') and [[Katori Jingū|Katori Shrine]] (香取神宮 ''Katori Jingū''). During the New Year period, from the first to the third of January, Kashima Shrine is visited by over 600,000 people from all over Japan{{fact|date=November 2023}}. It is the second most visited shrine in {{ill|Ibaraki Prefecture|en|Ibaraki Prefecture|qid=Q83273|lt=Ibaraki Prefecture|1=Ibaraki Prefecture}} for new year pilgrims.

==Introduction==
[[File:Kashima Shrine romon and stone lanterns - sept 22 2015.jpg|thumb|Romon gate and {{ill|Stone lantern|en|Stone lantern|qid=Q12012294|lt=stone lanterns|1=Stone lantern}}, 2015]]
[[File:Kashima-jingu honden.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Main Shrine]]
[[File:Kashima-jingu roumon.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{ill|Rōmon|en|Rōmon|qid=Q3458957|lt=Rōmon|1=Rōmon}}]]
[[File:Kashima jingu mitarashi panorama - sept 22 2015.jpg|thumb|Mitarashi (御手洗池) reflecting pond, 2015]]
Kashima Shrine is located at the top of the Kashima plateau in south-east {{ill|Ibaraki Prefecture|en|Ibaraki Prefecture|qid=Q83273|lt=Ibaraki Prefecture|1=Ibaraki Prefecture}}, intersecting {{ill|Lake Kasumigaura|en|Lake Kasumigaura|qid=Q1077984|lt=Lake Kitaura|1=Lake Kasumigaura}} and Kashima Bay and in close proximity to Katori Shrine, which also has a strong connection to the martial arts. The shrine is the home of the {{nihongo|{{ill|Kashima Shintō-ryū|en|Kashima Shintō-ryū|qid=Q4357180|lt=Kashima Shintō-ryū|1=Kashima Shintō-ryū}} |鹿島新当流|}} school of [[:en:Japanese swordsmanship|Japanese swordsmanship]]. {{nihongo|{{ill|Tsukahara Bokuden|en|Tsukahara Bokuden|qid=Q767236|lt=Tsukahara Bokuden|1=Tsukahara Bokuden}} |塚原 卜伝|extra= 1489 - March 6, 1571}}, one of the most distinguished swordmasters in Japanese history, was a frequent visitor to the shrine and developed the school from a combination of his own experiences as a ''shugyōsha'' during {{nihongo|[[Musha shugyō]]|武者修行|}}  and the {{nihongo|[[Tenshin Shōden Katori Shintō-ryū]] |天真正伝香取神道流|}}. 

A large blade designated as a [[:en:National Treasure of Japan|National Treasure]] known as the Futsu-no-Mitama Sword (布都御魂剣) is housed in the treasure house of Kashima Shrine. 

The ''[[Honden]]'' (main shrine building),  [[Haiden (Shinto)|''Haiden'']] (prayer hall) and ''{{ill|Rōmon|en|Rōmon|qid=Q3458957|lt=Rōmon|1=Rōmon}}'' tower gate entrance are all {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|qid=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}} structures, and are National [[:en:Important Cultural Property of Japan|Important Cultural Properties]]. The gate is one of the largest three shrine entrances in Japan. A deer enclosure is also located down the forest path. Both Kashima Shrine's deer and those of Nara are considered messengers of the gods and hence share a strong connection.
[[File:kashimadojo.jpg|thumb|Dojo inside Kashima Shrine, 2005]]

==Enshrined deity==
[[File:Kashima-kanameishi-shinzu-namazu-e.jpg|thumb|200px|right|「Kashima Keystone」(Ansei Era, 1855)<br/>The upper section of this illustration shows the stone in Kashima Shrine while below the god Takemikazuchi is pinning the giant catfish Ōnamazu with his sword.<br />[[Namazu|Ōnamazu]] (大鯰) is said to live below the islands of Japan and when aggravated is the cause of its many earthquakes. Takemikazuchi restrains the catfish through the use of the keystone.]]
[[File:The Famous Scenes of the Sixty States 21 Hitachi.jpg|thumb|[[Hiroshige]]]]
{{nihongo|Kashima Ōkami |鹿島大神|Kashima-no-Ōkami}} is the official title of the main enshrined deity and identified as {{nihongo|'''[[Takemikazuchi]]'''|武甕槌大神|}}. In some historical texts he is also known as the great god of thunder.

According to legend, [[Izanagi]], beheaded his own son [[Kagu-tsuchi|Kagutsuchi]] the fire deity, as punishment for burning his mother to death. As he performed the act the blood dripped from his sword splashing onto the rocks below him, giving birth to several ''kami'', two of which were Takemikazuchi along with {{nihongo|[[Futsunushi]]|経津主神| ''Futsunushi-no-kami''}} the deity of Katori Shrine. Per the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'', Takemikazuchi was the deity who provided {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|en|Emperor Jimmu|qid=Q200188|lt=Emperor Jimmu|1=Emperor Jimmu}} with a sword as he departed for the conquest of {{ill|Yamato Province|en|Yamato Province|qid=Q907495|lt=Yamato|1=Yamato Province}}, which is one reason the shrine is regarded as a patron. However, there is no mention of the shrine in either the ''Nihon Shoki'' or the ''[[Kojiki]]'' and the earliest written records, the ''Hitachi Fudoki'', does not identify the Kashima-no-Ōkami with Takemikazuchi.

==History==
[[File:Kashima the-great-torii.jpg|thumb|200px|right| The Torii Gate in 2008 before the 2011 earthquake]]
According the shrine legend, Kashima Jingū was established in the first year of the legendary {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|en|Emperor Jimmu|qid=Q200188|lt=Emperor Jimmu|1=Emperor Jimmu}}, i.e. 660 BC. This is well into Japanese prehistory, and the oldest written records mentioning the shrine are in the {{ill|Asuka period|en|Asuka period|qid=Q210688|lt=Asuka period|1=Asuka period}} [[Fudoki]] (風土記) of {{ill|Hitachi Province|en|Hitachi Province|qid=Q1055353|lt=Hitachi Province|1=Hitachi Province}}, indicating that a {{nihongo|''kobe''|神戸||}}, or private house of ritual was rebuilt in 649 AD on a site where the great celestial god {{nihongo|Kashima|香島の天の大神|Kashima-no-ten-no-Ōkami}} descended from the heavens and where religious ceremonies and festivals had been held since the time of {{ill|Emperor Sujin|en|Emperor Sujin|qid=Q333530|lt=Emperor Sujin|1=Emperor Sujin}}, {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|qid=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru|1=Yamato Takeru}} and {{ill|Emperor Tenji|en|Emperor Tenji|qid=Q314802|lt=Emperor Tenji|1=Emperor Tenji}}. This region was the ancestral stronghold of the [[Nakatomi clan]], who were strongly allied to the [[:en:Yamato dynasty|Yamato court]], and the area around Kashima became a center for strengthening the imperial court's control of eastern Japan following the [[Taika Reform]]. As both a war deity and a water deity, the Kashima ''kami'' were connected with military campaigns against the {{ill|Emishi|en|Emishi|qid=Q932574|lt=Emishi|1=Emishi}} tribes of northern Japan. The treasury of the shrine has a one bucket said to have been a war trophy once owned by the Emishi leader  {{ill|Aterui|en|Aterui|qid=Q1088046|lt=Aterui|1=Aterui}}.

During the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|qid=Q189178|lt=Nara period|1=Nara period}}, the Nakatomi clan rose to prominence and changed their name to [[Fujiwara clan|Fujiwara]] and played a central role in reorganizing the Shinto ritual system. By the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|qid=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, Kashima Jingū was given the highest Rank and the Shinto hierarchy, along with [[Ise Grand Shrine]] and Kashima Shrine. The ''[[Engishiki]]'' records list the shrine as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of Hitachi Province. Although the Fujiwara clan lost much of its power into the {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|qid=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period|1=Kamakura period}}, the shrine continued to enjoy high status and prestige with the warrior class and was strongly supported by successive  ''{{ill|Samurai|en|Samurai|qid=Q38142|lt=Samurai|1=Samurai}}'' governments and local ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]''. [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] granted the shrine numerous estates, and many members of the ''samurai'' class entered the [[kannushi|priesthood]], sometimes advancing to very senior positions. The shrine buildings were extensively reconstructed during the early {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|qid=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}, with {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|qid=Q171977|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu|1=Tokugawa Ieyasu}} sponsoring the reconstruction of the main shrine in 1605 (currently the main building of the Oku-no-miya Shrine),  {{ill|Tokugawa Hidetada|en|Tokugawa Hidetada|qid=Q314464|lt=Tokugawa Hidetada|1=Tokugawa Hidetada}} rebuilding the current main shrines in 1619 and with {{ill|Tokugawa Yorifusa|en|Tokugawa Yorifusa|qid=Q1133680|lt=Tokugawa Yorifusa|1=Tokugawa Yorifusa}} contributing the tower gate in 1634. In 1687, poet {{ill|Matsuo Bashō|en|Matsuo Bashō|qid=Q5676|lt=Matsuo Bashō|1=Matsuo Bashō}} traveled to the Kashima Shrine, writing of the journey in his ''{{ill|Haibun|en|Haibun|qid=Q728629|lt=Haibun|1=Haibun}}'' travel journal, ''{{ill|Kashima Kikō|en|Kashima Kikō|qid=Q112300304|lt=Kashima Kikō|1=Kashima Kikō}}''.

Following the [[Meiji Restoration|Meiji restoration]], the shrine was designated a {{nihongo|''[[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines#Kanpei-sha|Kanpei-sha]]''|官幣社}}, or imperial shrine, 1st Rank, under {{ill|State Shinto|en|State Shinto|qid=Q1197248|lt=State Shinto|1=State Shinto}}. The second ''torii'' gate was rebuilt in granite from {{ill|Kasama, Ibaraki|en|Kasama, Ibaraki|qid=Q845851|lt=Kasama|1=Kasama, Ibaraki}} in 1968 to celebrate the 100th anniversary of the Meiji restoration. The precincts of the shrine were designated a [[Monuments of Japan|National Historic Site]] in 1986.<ref name="Bunka1">{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/401/449 |title=鹿島神宮境内 附 郡家跡|trans-title=Kashima Jingū keidai tsuketari gūke ato|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}}</ref>

The shrine suffered only moderate damage in the {{ill|2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami|en|2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami|qid=Q36204|lt=2011 Tōhoku earthquake|1=2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami}}. The main ''torii'' gate was destroyed and 64 of the stone lanterns lining the shrine's pathways fell over. Although none of the main buildings were destroyed, the total cost of repairing the structures came to 170 million Yen. Following the earthquake, the first large scale [[archaeological excavation]] ever made on the site was conducted in the northwestern side of the precincts. Many artifacts dating back to the Nara period were uncovered.

==Grand Imperial Ofuna Festival==
This special festival held once every 12 years in the {{ill|Horse (zodiac)|en|Horse (zodiac)|qid=Q869595|lt=Year of the Horse|1=Horse (zodiac)}} is to honour the great deities Takemikazuchi of Kashima Shrine and Futsunushi of [[Katori Jingū|Katori Shrine]]. The festival is one of great pride for the people in the areas of Kashima and Katori and said to be one of the biggest in Japan. The next Grand Imperial Ofuna Festival will be in 2026.

The festival began during the time of {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|en|Emperor Ōjin|qid=Q317997|lt=Emperor Ōjin|1=Emperor Ōjin}} although it was stopped once during the civil warring of the {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|qid=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period|1=Muromachi period}} . In 1870, the tradition of the festival was revived and given imperial status. In 1887 it was decided that the festival would be held every 12 years in the Year of the Horse.

Today the Grand Imperial Ofuna festival begins in the morning on the first of September and officials from the imperial court are sent to convey the blessings of the Emperor. In the early morning of the second day a ''[[mikoshi]]'' (portable shrine) from Kashima Shrine is carried overland along the edge of Lake Kitaura, a smaller part of {{ill|Lake Kasumigaura|en|Lake Kasumigaura|qid=Q1077984|lt=Lake Kasumigaura|1=Lake Kasumigaura}}, to a large boat waiting in the harbor. The boat, adorned with a great Ryūtō (龍頭) dragon motif, then joins a larger fleet of other colourful boats (in 2002 there were around 90) and carries the ''mikoshi'' across the lake to the other side. From there a divine procession awaits to take the ''mikoshi'' to Katori Shrine where the main festival takes place. After the festival a special temporary logging known as an Angu (行宮) is constructed and the Mikoshi is taken there before being returned to its main shrine in the afternoon of the third day.

[[File:Kashima-jingu entrance.JPG|thumb]]
'''Kashima Jingu''' (鹿島神宮, pronounced “Kashima-jingū”) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|qid=Q845945|lt=Shinto Shrine|1=Shinto shrine}} located in {{ill|Ibaraki Prefecture|en|Ibaraki Prefecture|qid=Q83273|lt=Ibaraki Prefecture|1=Ibaraki Prefecture}}{{ill|Kashima, Ibaraki|en|Kashima, Ibaraki|qid=Q467471|lt=Kashima City|1=Kashima, Ibaraki}}{{ill|Miyachu (Kashima City)|ja|宮中 (鹿嶋市)|lt=Miyachu|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Miyachu (Kashima City)|1=Kyūchū|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11453223}}.
It is designated as a {{ill|Shikinaisha|ja|式内社|1=Shikinaisha|2=ja|3=式内社|1=Shikinaisha|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shikinaisha|13=User:Immanuelle|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyocho|lt=Shikinaisha}} ({{ill|Meishindaisya|ja|名神大社|fr|Myōjin Taisha|zh|名神大社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meishindaisya|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Myōjin Taisha|qid=Q9610964}}) and is the ichinomiya (primary shrine) of {{ill|Hitachi Province|en|Hitachi Province|qid=Q1055353|lt=Hitachi Province|1=Hitachi Province}}.
Under the former {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|en|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|comment=this used to link to modern system but that one is too overlinked|lt=Former Shrine Ranking|1=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines}}, it was Ranked as a {{ill|Kanpei Taisha|ja|官幣大社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kanpei Taisha|1=Kanpei Taisha (disambiguation)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q10209769}}; today, it is categorized as a {{ill|Beppyo shrine|en|Beppyo shrine|qid=Q10898274|lt=Beppyo Shrine|1=Beppyo shrine}} administered by the {{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|en|Association of Shinto Shrines|qid=Q908077|lt=Association of Shinto Shrines|1=Association of Shinto Shrines}}.

It is recognized as the head shrine of all the {{ill|Kashima Shrines|ja|鹿島神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kashima Shrines|qq=}} across Japan.
Together with {{ill|Katori Shrine|en|Katori Shrine|qid=Q372380|lt=Kasuga Jingu|1=Katori Jingū}} in {{ill|Chiba Prefecture|en|Chiba Prefecture|qid=Q80011|lt=Chiba Prefecture|1=Chiba Prefecture}}{{ill|Katori, Chiba|en|Katori, Chiba|qid=Q858357|lt=Katori City|1=Katori, Chiba}} and {{ill|Ikisu Jinja|ja|息栖神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ikisu Jinja|1=Ikisu Shrine|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11073095}} in {{ill|Kamisu|en|Kamisu|qid=Q840595|lt=Kamisu City|1=Kamisu}}, it is counted among the {{ill|Tōkoku San-sha|ja|東国三社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tōkoku San-sha|1=Tōgoku Sansha|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q17222093}}.<ref>[http://www.kamisu-kanko.jp/power/ {{bad link|These are causing so much issues|Tōkoku San-sha|ja|東国三社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tōkoku San-sha|qq=}}] (Kamisu City Tourism Association).</ref>
It is also revered through remote viewing (Yomigae) during the ritual known as {{ill|Shihōhai|ja|四方拝|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shihōhai|1=Shihohai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11419901}} at Miyachu.
== Overview ==
Situated in the southeastern part of Ibaraki Prefecture, Kashima Jingu is enshrined atop the Kashima Plateau between the {{ill|Kitaura|en|Kitaura|qid=Q11402369|lt=Kitauura|1=Kitaura}} and {{ill|Kashima-nada|ja|鹿島灘|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kashima-nada|1=Kashima Sea|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11677147}}. Its ancient foundation is attested in the ''Hitachi Fudoki'' and is regarded as the foremost ancient shrine in the eastern lands. The enshrined deity, {{ill|Takemikazuchi Ōkami|ja|武甕槌大神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takemikazuchi Ōkami|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to QID FIXED|qid=Q1502690|1=Takemikazuchi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q1502690}}, is celebrated in Japanese mythology as the divine warrior who played a pivotal role in the transfer of the realm from the great god Ōkuninushi during the subjugation of the land of Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni.

Because Hitachi marked the northern boundary of the early state, Kashima Jingu—with its patron deity who aided in subduing the land under the guidance of the heavenly grandchild—was venerated as the protector of the northern frontier.<ref>See, for example, “The Expansive Kamakura Period” by Yurika Tsuchiya, Bensei-sha, November 2024, p. 9 “Religion in Hitachi and the Mujudo” by Sumio Kameyama.</ref> In ancient times, it was esteemed by the imperial court as the divine force against the Emishi and later became revered as a tutelary deity by the Fujiwara clan. Its martial spirit endured through the medieval era when it was venerated as a war god by successive warrior regimes. Today, it continues to be deeply respected within martial arts circles.

== Name of the Shrine ==
Although the shrine is located in Hitachi Province’s Kashima District, the place name “Kashima” appears in the ''Hitachi Fudoki'' as “{{ill|Kashima (香島)|ja|香島|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kashima (香島)|1=koushima|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11667251}}”. In that text, the name “Kashima-gun” is explained as deriving from “the heavenly great deity of Kashima” (referring to Kashima Jingu). The earliest record of spelling “Kashima” as “鹿島” occurs in the 7th year of the Yōrō era (723 AD)<ref group="Primary Source">Excerpt from the ''Shoku Nihon Kōki'', Yōrō 7 (723 AD), November, Day 16.</ref> and by the early 8th century it appears to have been changed from “香島” to “鹿島”. Although the reason for this change is not clear from historical records, the shrine’s own tradition explains it as deriving from the sacred deer serving as its messenger.<ref>See official Kashima Jingu website’s “Deer Enclosure” page.</ref>

There are several theories regarding the origin of “Kashima”:
* One theory suggests that it comes from the word for “divine residence” (interpreted as “Kasumi”).
* Another posits that the name is derived from the deity {{ill|Takechikashima-no-mikoto|ja|建借間命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takechikashima-no-mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}.
* A further theory holds that it means “the place where the peg securing the moored ship is driven,” based on descriptions in the ''Hizen Fudoki''.<ref group="Primary Source">See the passage in the ''Hizen Fudoki'' concerning Kijima-gun.</ref>

Note that while the shrine uses the character for “島” (shima) in its name, the municipality of Kashima City in Ibaraki Prefecture uses the character “嶋” to distinguish itself from Kashima City in Saga Prefecture.
== The Enshrined Deity ==
[[File:Kashima-kanameishi-shinzu-namazu-e.jpg|thumb]]
The principal deity is a single kami:
* '''{{ill|Takemikazuchi Ōkami|ja|武甕槌大神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takemikazuchi Ōkami|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to QID FIXED|qid=Q1502690|1=Takemikazuchi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q1502690}}''' (read as “Takemikatsuchi no Ōkami”<ref name="Genealogy Documentation"/>/ “Takemikazuchi no Ōkami”<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu Chronicle|2004|p=8}}</ref>)
** In the ''Kojiki'', he is referred to as “Tatemikoto” (建御雷神), while in the ''Nihon Shoki'' he is written as “Takemikazuchi”.
** He is also known by the names “{{ill|Takefutsu no Kami|ja|建布都神|lt=Takefutsu|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takefutsu no Kami|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to QID FIXED|qid=Q1502690|1=Takemikazuchi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q1502690}}” and “{{ill|Toyofutsu no Kami|ja|豊布都神|lt=Toyofutsu|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyofutsu no Kami|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to QID FIXED|qid=Q1502690|1=Takemikazuchi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q1502690}}”.

=== About the Enshrined Deity ===
As indicated above, Kashima Jingu’s primary deity is Takemikazuchi. Regarding his origins, the ''Kojiki''<ref group="Primary Source" name="Kojiki">''Kojiki'', Kamiyo (Age of the Gods) section.</ref> narrates that when {{ill|Izanagi|ja|伊邪那岐命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izanagi|qid=Q813858}} severed the head of {{ill|Hinokagutsuchi|ja|火之迦具土神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hinokagutsuchi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to カグツチ|1=Kagu-tsuchi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q1640658}}, one of the three deities born from the blood that splattered upon the rock was Takemikazuchi.<ref group="Primary Source">''Nihon Shoki'', Kamiyo section.</ref> (In the ''Nihon Shoki'', it is said that at that moment, Mikahayahi – the progenitor of Takemikazuchi – was born.) Furthermore, before the descent of the heavenly grandchild, during the subjugation of Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni, Takemikazuchi is said to have acted alongside either the divine vessel god (as recounted in the ''Kojiki'') or {{ill|Futsunushi|en|Futsunushi|qid=Q1107286|lt=Keizutsushi-no-Kami|1=Futsunushi}} (as in the ''Nihon Shoki'').<ref>{{sfn|Higashi Minoru|2000|p=48}}</ref> Later, during Emperor {{ill|Jimmu's Eastern Expedition|en|Jimmu's Eastern Expedition|qid=Q11590444|lt=Jimmu’s eastern expedition|1=Jimmu's Eastern Expedition}}, Takemikazuchi presented the divine sword ({{ill|Futsunomitama|ja|布都御魂|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Futsunomitama|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Futsu-no-mitama|qid=Q11059754}}) to Iharibi, who is identified with Emperor {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|en|Emperor Jimmu|qid=Q200188|lt=Jimmu|1=Emperor Jimmu}}.<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu Chronicle|2004|p=8}}</ref> However, because neither the ''Kojiki'' nor the ''Nihon Shoki'' mention Kashima Jingu, the connection between Takemikazuchi and Kashima remains unclear.<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Shrine (Deities)|1984}}</ref>

On the other hand, the ''Hitachi Fudoki''<ref group="Primary Source" name="Fudoki"/> records the shrine’s deity as “{{ill|Kashima no Ama no Ōkami|ja|香島の天の大神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kashima no Ama no Ōkami|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}”, a deity said to have descended from heaven before the rule of the heavenly grandchild—an account reminiscent of the legends found in the ''Kojiki'' and ''Nihon Shoki''. Nonetheless, the Fudoki does not explicitly identify this deity with Takemikazuchi.<ref>{{sfn|Ichinomiya System|2000|p=230}}</ref>

The earliest document that identifies the shrine’s deity as Takemikazuchi appears in the ''Kogo Shūi''<ref group="Primary Source">''Kogo Shūi'' (see also {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}).</ref> (compiled in 807 AD), where it is stated “Regarding Takemikazuchi no Kami, Kashima in Hitachi is the one.”<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}</ref> Although the ''Engishiki'' (compiled in 927 AD) contains a “Kasuga Festival Prayer” that appears to mention “Kashima Zakan Mitama no Chikoto”, this prayer is believed by some scholars to date back to the foundation of Kasuga Taisha in the 2nd year of the Shingō era (768 AD)<ref name="Kasuga" group="Note"/>. Based on these sources, one theory holds that as the conquest of the Emishi advanced from the 8th century onward, the local deity “Kashima no Ama” gradually absorbed the martial attributes of Takemikazuchi from the central myth; another theory suggests that the very central myth of land transfer was devised by the Nakatomi clan, who interposed the local “Kashima no Ama” into the narrative.<ref>[https://www.books.example.com/matsumae Ken Matsumae, ''The Mysteries of Japanese Mythology'', Yamato Shobo, 2007, pp. 126-129]</ref> 

In summary, by virtue of the mythological accounts of Takemikazuchi’s role in subjugating the land and his donation of the divine weapon, the shrine’s deity came to be regarded as a war and martial god.<ref name="Heibonsha">{{sfn|Nishigaki Haruji, “Kashima Jingu”, in the World Encyclopedia, Heibonsha}}</ref> Particularly, regarding the alternate names “Takefutsu” or “Toyofutsu”, the term “Futsu” appears reminiscent of the name of the divine sword ({{ill|Futsunomitama|ja|布都御魂|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Futsunomitama|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Futsu-no-mitama|qid=Q11059754}}), which has led some to argue that he is a deity symbolizing the sharpness of blades.<ref name="Tatemikazuchi">{{sfn|Matsumae Ken, “Tatemikazuchi” in the National History Encyclopedia, Yoshikawa Kōbunkan}}</ref> As an expression of Kashima Jingu’s status as a war god, the poem from the late Heian period text ''Ryōjin Hishō'' which describes “the war god of the east of Seki, namely Kashima, Kasuga, and Suwa” is well known.<ref group="Primary Source">{{sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}</ref> Meanwhile, some accounts—drawing on the description in the Fudoki of the deities’ expedition by the diviners of the {{ill|Ujibe clan|ja|卜部氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ujibe clan|1=Urabe clan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11409028}} who allegedly dug a well—also point to an agricultural aspect of the deity.<ref>{{sfn|Fujisawa Akira|1994}}</ref> Viewed in total, these multiple facets (martial, maritime, and agricultural) have led some scholars to argue that the deity embodies a composite character.<ref>{{sfn|Fujisawa Akira|1994}}</ref> Furthermore, genealogical traditions connecting Takemikazuchi with the ancestral kami of the Nakatomi clan (such as {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|en|Ame-no-Koyane|qid=Q2564508|lt=Ame-no-Koyane|1=Ame-no-Koyane}} and others like {{ill|Ikatsumi no Mikoto|ja|津速産霊命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ikatsumi no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, {{ill|Ichikane no Mikoto|ja|市千魂命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ichikane no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, and {{ill|Raiden no Mikoto|ja|雷大臣命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Raiden no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 中臣烏賊津|1=Nakatomi no Ikatsu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q55536814}}) have given rise to theories that Takemikazuchi should be understood as the original thunder god of that clan.<ref>Takara Hisao, “On the Ancestors of the Nakatomi Clan and Their Divine Rituals,” in ''Studies in Ancient Clans V'', Seikosha, 2014, pp. 40–43.</ref>

== Characteristics ==
[[File:Katori-jingu haiden.JPG|thumb]] 
Kashima Jingu maintains a deep historical relationship with {{ill|Katori Shrine|en|Katori Shrine|qid=Q372380|lt=Kasuga Jingu|1=Katori Jingū}} (the ichinomiya of Shimousa Province, located in Kasatori City, Chiba Prefecture, with coordinates {{Coord|35|53|10.03|N|140|31|43.27|E|region:JP-12_type:landmark|name=Shimousa Ichinomiya: Kasuga Jingu}}). The two shrines, Kashima and Kasuga, have long been mentioned in tandem.
Both shrines have been venerated by the imperial court since ancient times, a devotion that is believed to stem from their roles as war deities.<ref>Supervised by the Association of Shinto Shrines, “The Basics of Shrines” (Fusosha), p. 76.</ref>

In ancient eastern Kantō, the coastal region (encompassing present-day {{ill|Lake Kasumigaura|en|Lake Kasumigaura|qid=Q1077984|lt=Kasumigaura|1=Lake Kasumigaura}}, Kitauura (formerly known as Nishiura or Kitauura), {{ill|Imba-numa|ja|印旛沼|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imba-numa|1=Inbanuma|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q5120731}}, and {{ill|Lake Tega|en|Lake Tega|qid=Q3215223|lt=Tegama-numa|1=Lake Tega}}) was once home to an inland sea called “Kasatori-kai.” The two shrines were strategically located at the gateway to this waterway, which is thought to have served as a transportation hub for the Yamato regime’s military expeditions against the Emishi.<ref name="Q5">{{ill|Yamamoto Hirofumi|ja|山本博文|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamamoto Hirofumi|1=Hirofumi Yamamoto|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11468918}}, “The History You Do Not Know of Chiba Prefecture” (Yōsen-sha) Q5 (pp. 26–27).</ref> Their branch shrines were enshrined across the northeastern coastline as symbols of the imperial court’s authority. The fact that the main shrine buildings of Kashima Jingu face north is also interpreted as an arrangement conscious of the Emishi in the north.<ref>{{sfn|Higashi Minoru|2000|p=26}}</ref>
== History ==

=== Founding and Tradition ===
According to Kashima Jingu’s own chronicle, the ''Kashima Kyūsha Reidenki'' (dating from the Kamakura period) and certain ancient documents (circa the 32nd year of the Ōei era, 1425 AD) report that the shrine’s first pillar was erected in the 1st year of Emperor {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|en|Emperor Jimmu|qid=Q200188|lt=Jimmu|1=Emperor Jimmu}}’s reign.<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu (Shikinaisha)|1976}}</ref> The shrine itself regards that year as its founding date.<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu Chronicle|2004|p=9}}</ref>

On the other hand, the ''Hitachi Fudoki''<ref group="Primary Source" name="Fudoki"/> also records a tradition in which the deity “{{ill|Kashima no Ama no Ōkami|ja|香島の天の大神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kashima no Ama no Ōkami|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}” descended from Takamagahara to the shrine at Kashima. Furthermore, this “Kashima no Ama no Ōkami” is said to be a collective name for the three shrines: the current Kashima Jingu (the main shrine), the shrine at Sakado (currently the Sessha Sakado Jinja), and the shrine at Numao (currently the Sessha Numao Jinja). Later, during the reign of Emperor {{ill|Emperor Sujin|en|Emperor Sujin|qid=Q333530|lt=Sujin|1=Emperor Sujin}} (the 10th generation), the noble Ōnakatomi Kamikitamiki received a divine oracle from Kashima on Mount Ōsaka, prompting the emperor to present weapons, horse gear, and other items.<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu (Shikinaisha)|1982}}</ref> In the time of Emperor {{ill|Emperor Keikō|en|Emperor Keikō|qid=Q329723|lt=Keikō|1=Emperor Keikō}} (the 12th generation), the noble {{ill|Nakatomi Sayo-no-mikoto|ja|臣狭山命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakatomi Sayo-no-mikoto|1=Omikiyama no Mikoto|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q99517230}} is said to have offered three boats in response to another oracle from the deity—a ritual that is considered the origin of the Ship Festival ({{ill|Mifune-sai|ja|御船祭|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mifune-sai|1=Q11489285|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11489285}}).<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu (Shikinaisha)|1982}}</ref>

Nakatomi Sayo-no-mikoto had participated in the eastern expedition of {{ill|Yowatari no Mikoto|ja|倭建命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yowatari no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ヤマトタケル|1=Yamato Takeru|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q461258}}, and the distribution of Kashima and its branch deities in the Mutsu region is thought to be due to the participation of his ancestors or members of his retinue in that campaign. Some scholars even argue that the boats recorded in the Fudoki were actually offerings presented during Yowatari no Mikoto’s eastern expedition.<ref name="#1">Takara Hisao, “On the Early Phase of the Nakatomi Clan—Ancestors of the Nakatomi and Ujibe Clans,” in ''Studies in Ancient Clans V'', Seikosha, 2014, pp. 35–37.</ref>

=== Overview of Historical Phases ===

==== Asuka Period ====
The ''Hitachi Fudoki''<ref group="Primary Source" name="Fudoki"/> recounts that numerous auxiliary worship units ({{ill|Jinkabe|ja|神戸|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jinkabe|1=Kobe|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11589706}}) were established at Kashima to maintain its ritual functions.<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu (Shikinaisha)|1982}}</ref> According to the Fudoki, in the 5th year of the Taika era (649 AD), the Kashima District was established as a divine district, and during the reign of Emperor {{ill|Emperor Tenji|en|Emperor Tenji|qid=Q314802|lt=Tenji|1=Emperor Tenji}} (668–672 AD), the first envoy was dispatched for the construction work. This is generally understood as part of the new governmental reforms following the Taika Reforms, when the court intensified its administration of the eastern provinces and deepened its ties with Kashima Jingu.<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu (Shikinaisha)|1982}}</ref>

The close association with the imperial court was facilitated by the rise of the Nakatomi clan, which reorganized ritual institutions in the late 6th to early 7th century and thereby came to control the worship at this once-local shrine. Indeed, historical records show that many officials holding the post of district head or shrine priest bore the Nakatomi name.<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu (Shikinaisha)|1982}}</ref> In the wake of the Taika Reforms, the Nakatomi clan’s political ascendancy is reflected in Kashima Jingu’s growing importance as a court shrine.<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu (Shikinaisha)|1982}}</ref> (The details regarding the pre-Nakatomi ritual clans remain subject to various theories; see the “Research” section below.)

==== Nara Period ====
[[File:Kasuga-taisha11bs3200.jpg|thumb]] 
During the Nara period, numerous entries concerning auxiliary worship units ({{ill|Jinkabe|ja|神戸|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jinkabe|1=Kobe|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11589706}}) appear in the chronicles (see the “Shrine Domain” section). In this era, Kashima Jingu was particularly revered as the tutelary deity by the Fujiwara clan. In the 2nd year of the {{ill|Jingo-keiun|en|Jingo-keiun|qid=Q1373049|lt=Shingō|1=Jingo-keiun}} era (768 AD), it is recorded that a shrine (later known as Kasuga Jingu) was founded at Kasuga (located on Mount Migamine in Nara Prefecture) as the tutelary shrine of the Fujiwara clan; during this event, the deities from Kashima (the primary deity), Kasuga (the secondary deity representing {{ill|Keizutsushi-no-Kami|ja|経津主命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keizutsushi-no-Kami|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to QID FIXED|qid=Q1107286|1=Futsunushi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q1107286}}), and from Hiraoka (the tertiary deity, {{ill|Amanoyane no Mikoto|ja|天児屋根命|1=Ame-no-Koyane|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amanoyane no Mikoto|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Koyane|qid=Q2564508}}, later Ranked as the fourth deity) were enshrined.<ref name="Kasuga">{{ill|Inagaki Eizō|ja|稲垣栄三|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inagaki Eizō|1=Eizō Inagaki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11596499}}, “Kasuga Jingu” in ''National History Encyclopedia'', Yoshikawa Kōbunkan.</ref> Among these, Kashima’s deity was considered the principal one, and it is thought that the original ritual of Kasuga was initiated as a remote worship (Yomigae) of Kashima Jingu.<ref name="Kasuga"/>
Subsequently, the relationship with the Fujiwara clan remained strong; for example, in the 8th year of the {{ill|Hōki|en|Hōki|qid=Q18520676|lt=Hōki|1=Hōki}} era (777 AD), during the illness of Fujiwara no Yoshitsugu,<ref group="Primary Source" name="Hōki8"/> a court Rank of Senior Third was conferred upon Kashima Jingu’s tutelary deity.<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu (Kakudō)|1983}}</ref>

==== Heian Period ====
From the Heian period onward, the deity’s court Rank is attested as follows: in the 3rd year of {{ill|Jōwa|en|Jōwa|qid=Q3577279|lt=Shōwa|1=Jōwa}} (836 AD), the deity was awarded the Rank of Junior Second, First Class Merit, which was later elevated to Senior Second, First Class Merit; in the 6th year of Shōwa (839 AD), the Rank of Junior First, First Class Merit is recorded.<ref group="Primary Source" name="Shōwa3">{{sfn|Kashima Jingu (Shikinaisha)|1982}}</ref> In the 3rd year of {{ill|Kashō|en|Kashō|qid=Q1373157|lt=Kashō|1=Kashō}} (850 AD), it is said that the deity reached the Rank of Senior First (or possibly Senior First, First Class Merit), an honor that is also believed to have been concurrently bestowed upon the enshrined deity at Kashima.<ref name="Kashō3">{{sfn|Kashima Jingu (Shikinaisha)|1982}}</ref>

The ''Engishiki'' (established in 927 AD) in its “Shinmei-cho” section lists Kashima Jingu (located in Kashima District, Ibaraki Prefecture) as “Kashima Jingu, Meishindaisya, Tsukiji Shin-narate” and records that in the Tsukiji Festival and the New Rice Festival, ritual offerings of cloth and other items were made.<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu (Shikinaisha)|1982}}</ref> It is noteworthy that, in the Engishiki, only three shrines (the Great Shrine of Ise, Kashima Jingu, and Kasuga Jingu) are designated with the title “Jingū”. Furthermore, within Hitachi Province, Kashima came to be regarded as the ichinomiya (the primary shrine).<ref group="Note">The first known use of the term “ichinomiya” dates to the 3rd year of Kenryaku (1213 AD). {{Harvnb|Ichinomiya System|2000|p=230}}</ref>

==== From the Kamakura Period to the Edo Period ====
Kashima Jingu, as a shrine enshrining a war god, continued to be esteemed during the medieval era by the warrior class. It received many offerings of ritual money and land donations from the samurai, as evidenced by numerous historical records.<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu (Shikinaisha)|1982}}</ref> On the other hand, there were also frequent incursions by the warrior class into the shrine’s priestly offices and violations of its territorial domain.<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu (Shikinaisha)|1982}}</ref> For instance, when Minamoto no Yoritomo appointed a member of the Kashima clan (a branch of the Hitachi Ōmoshi clan) as an assistant to the shrine’s head priest (Omochibari), the shrine gradually moved out of Fujiwara influence.<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu (Shikinaisha)|1982}}</ref> In the Muromachi period, while contributions of land by the warrior governments continued, local power holders also increasingly encroached upon the shrine’s domain, leading to chronic financial difficulties for the shrine’s reconstruction projects.

==== Edo Period ====
During the Edo period, Kashima Jingu received high imperial patronage from the Edo Shogunate. In the 10th year of {{ill|Keichō|en|Keichō|qid=Q1328185|lt=Keichō|1=Keichō}} (1605 AD), Tokugawa Ieyasu oversaw the construction of a new main hall (now the Sessha Okugū’s shrine building). Later, in the 5th year of {{ill|Yuanhe|en|Yuanhe|qid=Q10889567|lt=Genna|1=Yuanhe}} (1619 AD), Tokugawa Hidetada had the entire shrine complex rebuilt, and in the 11th year of {{ill|Kan'ei|en|Kan'ei|qid=Q1192913|lt=Kannen|1=Kan'ei}} (1634 AD), Tokugawa Yorifusa oversaw the construction of the roof gate (rōmon) and other structures.<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu (Shikinaisha)|1982}}</ref>

==== Modern Times (Meiji Period Onward) ====
After the Meiji Restoration, in the 4th year of Meiji (1871 AD) under the modern shrine Ranking system, Kashima Jingu was designated as a {{ill|Kanpei Taisha|ja|官幣大社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kanpei Taisha|1=Kanpei Taisha (disambiguation)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q10209769}}.<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu Chronicle|2004|p=153}}</ref> In the postwar period, it has been classified as a {{ill|Beppyo shrine|en|Beppyo shrine|qid=Q10898274|lt=Beppyo Shrine|1=Beppyo shrine}} under the Association of Shinto Shrines.

In 1968 (Showa 43), as a centennial commemoration of the Meiji Restoration, a new great torii (the secondary torii) was rebuilt using granite from Kasama City, Ibaraki Prefecture.<ref name="Tokyo Shimbun"/> In 1986 (Showa 61), the shrine grounds were designated as a National Historic Site.<ref name="Historic Site"/> Subsequently, on March 11, 2011, the Great Stone Torii (the secondary torii) and the torii of the Mitarai Pond collapsed due to the Tōhoku-Pacific Ocean Earthquake and its aftershocks; in addition, 64 stone lanterns and the main hall’s chigi sustained damage, with total damages amounting to 107 million yen.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Elegant Stillness and Motion: The Autumn Festival Begins on the 1st and 2nd of Next Month – A Traditional, Heian-Era Scroll-like Celebration|newspaper=Ibaraki Shimbun |date=2013-08-29 |edition=Morning Edition |page=16}}</ref><ref>{{Citation|url=http://city.kashima.ibaraki.jp/info/detail.php?no=5792|title=Record of the March 11, 2011 Tōhoku Earthquake|publisher=Kashima City|date=June 2012|page=3|accessdate=2014-07-23}}</ref> Later, a new great torii was rebuilt using locally sourced cedar; its Completion ceremony was held in June 2014 (Showa 26).<ref name="Tokyo Shimbun"/>
== Shrine Complex ==
The site on which the shrine is located is known as “{{ill|Mikasayama|ja|三笠山|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mikasayama|1=Q10866570|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q10866570}}” (“Mikasa Mountain”). This sacred precinct is designated as a National Historic Site because of its significance in Japan’s history (including the grounds of Sessha Sakado Jinja, Sessha Numao Jinja, and the remnants of the Kashima District ruling family site).<ref name="Historic Site"/>
The total area of the shrine grounds is approximately 70 hectares,<ref name="Genealogy Documentation">Kashima Jingu Shrine Chronicle.</ref> of which about 40 hectares is a dense forest known as the “Kashima Jingu Forest,” designated by Ibaraki Prefecture as a Natural Monument.<ref name="Forest"/><ref name="Ibaraki Shimbun"/>
Within this woodland, roughly 800 species of plants flourish; many ancient giant trees are found here, making it one of the region’s most prominent evergreen broad-leaved forests.<ref name="Forest"/>

=== Shrine Buildings ===
[[File:Kashima-jingu honden.JPG|thumb]]
[[File:Kashima-jingu karidono.JPG|thumb]]
[[File:Kashima-jingu roumon.JPG|thumb]][[File:Kashima-jingu shasou.JPG|thumb]]
The principal shrine buildings consist of the main hall, the “stone room” (the corridor connecting the main hall and the rear offering hall), the offering hall, and the worship hall. All of these structures date from the early Edo period – specifically, from the 5th year of the Genna era (1619 AD) – and were constructed under the orders of Tokugawa Hidetada, the second shogun of the Edo Shogunate, by master carpenter Nagasawa Chōji. The offering hall was built behind the worship hall and is connected to the main hall by a corridor known as the “stone room.” Although the approach to the shrine extends straight east from the roof gate, the shrine buildings themselves are positioned offset toward the south; as a result, the main hall faces north. This arrangement is said to have been designed with the northern Emishi in mind.<ref name="Main Hall"/><ref>{{sfn|Higashi Minoru|2000|p=27}}</ref> (It is noted, however, that in some early examples the main hall’s configuration was set transversely relative to the viewer, in accordance with ancient palace designs.<ref>See Masayuki Miura, “The Main Halls of Shrines – The Divine Space as Revealed by Architecture,” Yoshikawa Kōbunkan, 2013, pp. 182–189.</ref>)

The main hall ({{ill|Honden|en|Honden|qid=Q2044994|lt=Honden|1=Honden}}) is a three-bay structure in the Nagare-zukuri style with a single bay for the forward worship and is roofed with cypress bark. Its pillars and structural members are lavishly decorated with lacquer and vivid pigments.<ref name="Main Hall"/> Prior to the construction of the present main hall in Genna 5 (1619 AD), the building now known as the Okugū (rear shrine) had served as the main hall. Although the main hall faces north, its inner sanctuary (naijin) is located in the southwestern corner, so that worshippers do not directly face the deity but instead view it to the east (see diagram below). Some scholars have noted a resemblance to the main hall of {{ill|Izumo-taisha|en|Izumo-taisha|qid=Q696362|lt=Izumo Taisha|1=Izumo-taisha}}.<ref>{{sfn|Higashi Minoru|2000|p=27}}</ref> In earlier times the main hall was known as the “Unopened Palace” (akazuno goten), and it was said that its doors were opened only on January 7 each year during the ritual in which the offering hall’s objects were exchanged by the priest of the Monoomi; this tradition is recounted in the ''Kashima Kyūsha Reidenki''. <ref>{{sfn|Kashima Monoomi (National History)|1983}}</ref> Behind the main hall stands a sacred tree (shinboku), a giant cedar measuring 43 meters in height with a root spread of 12 meters and an estimated age of about 1,000 years.<ref name="Forest"/> Further back, separated by a stone wall (tamagaki), lies a stone known as the “Mirror Stone” (kagami-ishi) about 80 centimeters in diameter, which is traditionally regarded as the location of the shrine’s founding.<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu (Shikinaisha)|1982}}</ref>

The “stone room” is a structure with two ken (bay lengths) across the eaves, one ken between the beams, single-storied, of a gabled (kirizuma) construction with a cypress bark roof, and its front side adjoins the offering hall. Like the main hall, it is richly decorated with lacquer and vivid pigments. The offering hall is similarly constructed with two ken by one ken dimensions, of gabled (kirizuma) style with a cypress bark roof, and it adjoins the worship hall. The worship hall is a five-ken structure with three ken between the beams, one-storied, built in the irimoya style with one ken for forward worship and roofed with cypress bark. Unlike the main hall, stone room, and offering hall, the worship hall and offering hall have a simpler design without lacquer or vivid pigments, remaining in plain wood. All of these structures (the main hall, stone room, offering hall, and worship hall) have been designated as National Important Cultural Properties.<ref name="Main Hall"/>
To the right of the worship hall, facing south, stands the temporary hall (karidono), also referred to as the “Gondō.” It was built at the time the new main hall was constructed in Genna 5 (1619 AD) by the same master carpenter, Nagasawa Chōji, to temporarily house the divine spirit during the reconstruction process. Structurally, it is a three-ken building with two ken between the beams, one-storied, built in the irimoya style with one ken for forward worship and roofed with cypress bark. Although its design is relatively simple owing to its temporary nature, portions of it are adorned with lacquer decorations. Originally, it is said to have been located to the left of the worship hall, facing west, but after several relocations it was fixed in its current position in 1951 (Showa 26). This temporary hall is also designated as a National Important Cultural Property.<ref name="Karidono"/>

On the approach to the shrine within the grounds stands the roof gate (rōmon), which is counted among “Japan’s Three Great Roof Gates”.<ref name="Three Great Roof Gates" group="Note">“Japan’s Three Great Roof Gates” are said to be the roof gates of Kashima Jingu, {{ill|Aso Shrine|en|Aso Shrine|qid=Q715639|lt=Aso Jinja|1=Aso Shrine}} (Aso City, Kumamoto Prefecture), and {{ill|Hakozaki Shrine|en|Hakozaki Shrine|qid=Q714742|lt=Hakozaki Shrine|1=Hakozaki Shrine}} (Fukuoka City, Fukuoka Prefecture).</ref> The rōmon was originally built in the 11th year of {{ill|Kan'ei|en|Kan'ei|qid=Q1192913|lt=Kan’ei|1=Kan'ei}} (1634 AD) by Tokugawa Yorifusa, the first daimyō of Mito Domain, with construction overseen by the carpenters of Echizen, Yoshimasa Sakagami. Its structure is two-storied in the irimoya style with three ken in width (excluding the doorway), and although it is now roofed with copper plates, it was originally cypress bark–roofed. The overall design is boldly coated in vermilion lacquer, with only minimal ornamentation on features such as the transoms. The horizontal scroll bearing the inscription “Kashima Torii” is by {{ill|Tōgō Heihachirō|en|Tōgō Heihachirō|qid=Q296785|lt=Tōgō Heihachirō|1=Tōgō Heihachirō}}. The corridors flanking the rōmon were built at the same time, though additional marker posts were later added. The rōmon is designated as a National Important Cultural Property, and its corridors are recognized as Kashima City–designated cultural properties.<ref name="Roof Gate"/>

At the entrance to the shrine stands the “Great Torii” – a massive wooden gate constructed using four giant cedars. Its dimensions are approximately 10.2 meters in height and 14.6 meters in width. Originally, it was a stone torii built from granite sourced in Kasama City; however, on March 11, 2011, during the Tōhoku-Pacific Ocean Earthquake and its aftershocks, the torii collapsed from its base. In response, four giant cedars were felled from the shrine grounds and used to rebuild the torii – marking the 11th reconstruction since records began in 1664. The design features two cylindrical columns surmounted by a log-like horizontal lintel, with square-shaped crossbeams projecting from the outside of the columns. This form is known as the “Kashima Torii”.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Kashima Torii|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E9%B9%BF%E5%B3%B6%E9%B3%A5%E5%B1%85-462179|work=Digital Daijisen|accessdate=2014-07-23}}</ref> The cedars used have estimated ages of approximately 500 years for the left and right columns, about 600 years for the lintel, and about 250 years for the crossbeam. The foundation stone (kamebaraishi) incorporates remnants of the collapsed torii.<ref name="Tokyo Shimbun">{{Cite news |title=Natural Monument: Traditional Wooden Torii Rebuilt from Shrine Cedars – Three Years after the Quake, Kashima Jingu’s Great Torii Revived; Head Priest Expresses Gratitude to Ancestors and the Deity|newspaper=Tokyo Shimbun |date=2014-06-01 |edition=Morning, Ibaraki Edition |page=24}}</ref>

== Festivals ==
=== Cycle Festivals (Shikinen Sai) ===
Every 12 years, the grand festival known as the {{ill|Mifune-sai|ja|御船祭|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mifune-sai|1=Q11489285|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11489285}} (Ship Festival) is held, which is the largest maritime festival in Japan and marks the meeting of the deities of Kashima Jingu and Kasuga Jingu on the water. According to tradition, this festival was established during the time of Emperor {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|en|Emperor Ōjin|qid=Q317997|lt=Ojin|1=Emperor Ōjin}}, though it was suspended during the Sengoku period and later revived in 1870 (Meiji 3).<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu (Shikinaisha)|1982}}</ref>

The sequence of rituals is as follows:<ref>{{sfn|Mifune-sai (Kashima Jingu Official Site)|—}}</ref>
* On the morning of September 1, an imperial envoy ({{ill|Chokushi|ja|勅使|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chokushi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Chokushi|qid=Q11399920}}) arrives to commence the grand annual festival.
* Early on September 2, a portable shrine (mikoshi) departs from Kashima Jingu and reaches the coastal area at Ōfuna (located along the northern shore of Kasumigaura) by land. There, the mikoshi is transferred onto a decorated ceremonial boat ({{ill|Gosabune|ja|御座船|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gosabune|1=gozabune|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11489006}}) along with numerous auxiliary boats. It then makes its way by water to Kasatori in Kamatori City, where it receives a welcoming ceremony from Kasuga Jingu, before retracing its route back to the temporary palace.
* In the afternoon of September 3, the procession returns from the temporary palace to the main hall.

; Hakuba Festival
: Called “Hakuba-sai”. Held on January 7 as a medium-scale ceremony.
: In earlier times the shrine observed a custom of refraining from festivals from New Year’s Day through the 6th, under the belief that the enshrined deity was asleep; on January 7, the main hall (then known as the “Unopened Palace”) would be opened by the priest of the Monoomi for a ritual in which the door was unlocked. During that ceremony, a white horse was quietly paraded for the purpose of exorcising evil, although over time the sound of the key striking became louder and the horse was driven more roughly. While the door-unlocking ritual is no longer performed, the event is now celebrated as the “Hakuba Festival,” during which a white horse races from the eastern gate to the roof gate.<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu Chronicle|2004|pp=29–32}}</ref>
; Saitō Festival
: Called “Saitō-sai”. Held on March 9 as a grand ceremony.
: It is said to have originated during the time of Emperor {{ill|Tenmu|ja|Emperor Tenmu|1=Emperor Tenmu|2=ja|3=天武天皇|1=Emperor Tenmu|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenmu|13=User:Immanuelle/Emperor Tenmu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q335181}}, re-enacting the posture of the guards when forming a “Kashima Stand” (Kashima-dachi). The festival is conducted by two groups chosen by divination from among the 66 local districts (24 northern and 26 southern districts in present-day configuration). Dressed in colorful garments led by a child of about 5 years old (the Shibochi), a lively procession known as the “Saitō Bayashi” is performed before reaching the main hall.<ref name="Saitō-sai">{{sfn|Kashima Jingu (Shikinaisha)|1976}}</ref> This festival has been selected as an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property by the national government.<ref name="Saitō-sai"/>
Note: Until the Meiji period, the festival rites at Kashima Jingu were performed outdoors; since then they have been moved indoors.
== Divine Treasures ==
Here we introduce two of the shrine’s most venerated treasures; for details on other treasures, please refer to the “Cultural Properties” section.

=== Futsunomitama Sword ===
[[File:Isonokami-jingu, haiden-2.jpg|thumb]] 
The '''Futsunomitama Sword''' (ふつのみたまのつるぎ), also known as the “Hirakuni Sword” (平国剣), is the sacred sword preserved at Kashima Jingu.<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu Chronicle|2004|p=70}}</ref> It is designated as a National Treasure; its full official designation is “Chokutō – Kuro Urushi Hyōmon Daidachigoshirae, with an attached sword cabinet.”<ref name="Chokutō">{{国指定文化財等データベース|201|467|Chokutō: Kuro Urushi Hyōmon Daidachigoshirae}}</ref> For centuries it was kept hidden within the inner sanctuary of the main hall.<ref name="Chokutō"/>
This exceptionally long straight sword measures 2.71 meters in total length (including the handle and scabbard) with a blade length of 2.24 meters. Although its precise date of manufacture is unknown, the blade is believed to date from the Nara to Heian period, while the mounting is thought to be from the Heian period.<ref name="Chokutō"/> It is one of the oldest extant Japanese swords (that is not an archaeological find) and is considered the longest surviving sword. To achieve such an extended blade length, the sword was constructed using a rare technique of joining four sections together. The fittings (handle and scabbard) are decorated in an ancient style with black lacquer, inlaid with thin sheets (hyoumon) of gold and silver and ornamented with metal fittings made with a copper and bronze openwork technique – reflecting the tradition of the “Kin Gin Densō Tō” housed in Shōsōin.
In the ''Kojiki'' and ''Nihon Shoki'', the sword is also mentioned under the names “Futsunomitama Sword” or “Futsunomitama Ken” and is described as the divine sword handed by Takemikazuchi to the progenitor of Emperor {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|en|Emperor Jimmu|qid=Q200188|lt=Jimmu|1=Emperor Jimmu}} via {{ill|Takemikazuchi Ōkami|ja|武甕槌神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takemikazuchi Ōkami|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to QID FIXED|qid=Q1502690|1=Takemikazuchi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q1502690}} through {{ill|Takakuraji|en|Takakuraji|qid=Q11668757|lt=Takakurashimo|1=Takakuraji}}. After Emperor Jimmu’s enthronement, the sword was enshrined in the palace and later transferred to Izumo Taisha during the reign of Emperor {{ill|Emperor Sujin|en|Emperor Sujin|qid=Q333530|lt=Sujin|1=Emperor Sujin}}.<ref>Ōba Iwao, “Izumo Taisha,” in the National History Encyclopedia, Yoshikawa Kōbunkan.</ref> The Futsunomitama sword preserved at Kashima Jingu is said to have been remade in later times because the original, once destined to return to Kashima, never did so.<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu Chronicle|2004|pp=70–72}}</ref> Its forging is also connected by some scholars with the tradition recorded in the ''Hitachi Fudoki'' that a sword was made from sand iron.
=== Hitachi Obi ===
The '''Hitachi Obi''' (ひたちおび) is another sacred treasure of the shrine.<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu Chronicle|2004|p=72}}</ref> According to tradition, it is the girdle that Empress {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|qid=Q232803|lt=Jingū|1=Empress Jingū}} offered in gratitude for Kashima Jingu’s protection during her conquest of the Three Kingdoms of Korea.<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu Chronicle|2004|p=148}}</ref> For many generations it was stored deep within the main hall’s inner box and remains hidden from public view.<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu Chronicle|2004|p=72}}</ref>

== Cultural Properties ==
=== National Treasures ===
* Chokutō – Kuro Urushi Hyōmon Daidachigoshirae (attached to a sword cabinet) (Craftsman’s work)
** Commonly known as the “Futsunomitama Sword”. Designated on June 22, Showa 30.<ref name="Chokutō">{{国指定文化財等データベース|201|467|Chokutō: Kuro Urushi Hyōmon Daidachigoshirae}}</ref>

=== Important Cultural Properties (National Designation) ===
* The main hall, stone room, worship hall, and offering hall (four structures, with two accompanying plaque tablets) (Buildings) – the main hall was designated on March 27, Meiji 34, and the other three on April 17, Meiji 44.<ref name="Main Hall">{{国指定文化財等データベース|102|249|Kashima Jingu > Main Hall}}</ref><ref>{{国指定文化財等データベース|102|250|Kashima Jingu > Stone Room}}</ref><ref>{{国指定文化財等データベース|102|251|Kashima Jingu > Offering Hall}}</ref><ref>{{国指定文化財等データベース|102|252|Kashima Jingu > Worship Hall}}</ref><ref>[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/kuni/kenzou/1-1/1-1.html Kashima Jingu Main Hall, Worship Hall, Offering Hall, and Stone Room (with plaque tablets)] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education)</ref><ref group="Note">On September 17, Showa 29, the “Kashima Jingu Main Hall” and “Kashima Jingu Worship, Offering, and Stone Room” were merged as one set designated “Kashima Jingu 4 Structures”. Refer to “List of National Treasures and Important Cultural Properties – Buildings”, Preservation Society for Architectural Technology, 1996; “Catalog of National Treasures and Important Cultural Properties – Buildings”, Daiichi Hōki, 1990.</ref>
* The Okugū (rear shrine main hall) of the Sessha – designated on March 27, Meiji 34.<ref>{{国指定文化財等データベース|102|253|Kashima Jingu Sessha Okugū Main Hall}}</ref><ref name="Okugū">[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/kuni/kenzou/1-2/1-2.html Kashima Jingu Sessha Okugū Main Hall (with plaque)] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education)</ref>
* The rōmon (roof gate) – designated on June 11, Showa 41.<ref name="Roof Gate">{{国指定文化財等データベース|102|254|Kashima Jingu Rōmon}}<br />[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/kuni/kenzou/1-12/1-12.html Kashima Jingu Rōmon] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education)</ref>
* The karidono (temporary hall) – designated on May 20, Showa 51.<ref name="Karidono">{{国指定文化財等データベース|102|255|Kashima Jingu Karidono}}<br />[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/kuni/kenzou/1-23/1-23.html Kashima Jingu Karidono] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education)</ref>
* A pair of ume-take makie saddles (with four-hand makie inlaid wood; crafted items)
** Attributed to the Kamakura period, they are considered the oldest examples of makie saddles in Japan. According to the shrine tradition, they are identified in the ''Agatsuma Kagami'' (compiled in {{ill|Kenkyū 2|ja|建久2年|lt=Year 2 of Kenkyū|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kenkyū 2|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, 1191 AD) as military saddles donated by Minamoto no Yoritomo; however, their style is distinct from ordinary military saddles, and they are believed to have been used in festivals. They were designated on June 27, Showa 34.<ref>{{国指定文化財等データベース|201|5891|Ume-take Makie Saddle}}</ref>

=== National Historic Sites ===
* The Kashima Jingu precincts with the remnants of the Kashima District ruling family – designated on August 4, Showa 61, with additional designations in subsequent years (first in Heisei 1, then Heisei 11, 13, 17, and 20).<ref name="Historic Site">{{国指定文化財等データベース|401|449|Kashima Jingu Grounds with Ruling Family Remains}}<br />[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/kuni/shiseki/12-20/12-20.html Kashima Jingu Grounds with Ruling Family Remains] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education)</ref>
** This designation covers four sites: within the Kashima Jingu precincts, the grounds of Sessha Sakado Jinja, the grounds of Sessha Numao Jinja, and the Kashima District ruling family site.
=== Selected Important Intangible Folk Cultural Properties (National Selection) ===
* The “Kashima Saitō Festival” – selected on December 25, Showa 51.<ref name="Saitō-sai">[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/mingei/17-6/17-6.html Kashima Saitō Festival] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education)</ref>

=== Ibaraki Prefecture–Designated Cultural Properties ===
[[File:Kashima-jingu tourou.JPG|thumb]]
[[File:Kashima-jingu shasou.JPG|thumb]]
* Tangible Cultural Properties:
** Two wooden guardian dog statues (komainu) – from the early Edo period, dating to Genna 5 (1619 AD); one pair measures approximately 77.3 cm (A-type) and 80.3 cm (Un-type) in height respectively; designated on July 23, Showa 33.<ref>[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/ken/tyokoku/3-24/3-24.html Wooden Komainu] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education)</ref>
** Two additional wooden komainu – attributed to the Kamakura period, approximately 72 cm in height each; designated on February 24, Showa 40.<ref>[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/ken/tyokoku/3-52/3-52.html Wooden Komainu] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education)</ref>
** One black lacquered, raden makie display stand; from the late Kamakura period; designated on July 23, Showa 33.<ref>[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/ken/kougei/4-23/4-23.html Black Lacquered Raden Makie Stand] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education)</ref>
** One bronze seal – from the Heian period, bearing the inscription “Shintatada In”; examples of such seals appear in documents from 1341 (Rekiō 4); designated on July 23, Showa 33.<ref>[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/ken/kougei/4-24/4-24.html Bronze Seal] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education)</ref>
** Three ceramic komainu – attributed to the Muromachi period; designated on July 23, Showa 33.<ref>[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/ken/kougei/4-25/4-25.html Ceramic Komainu] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education)</ref>
** One stone lantern – from the early Edo period (Genna 5, 1619 AD), with a total height of 256 cm; designated on July 23, Showa 33.<ref>[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/ken/kougei/4-26/4-26.html Stone Lantern] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education)</ref>
** One bell (shō) – from the early Heian period, one of a set of three-pronged bells; designated on July 23, Showa 33.<ref>[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/ken/kougei/4-27/4-27.html Bell] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education)</ref>
** One military battle standard (gunpai) – from the Muromachi period; designated on July 23, Showa 33.<ref>[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/ken/kougei/4-28/4-28.html Gunpai] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education)</ref>
** One tachi (long sword) by the Bizen swordsmith Kageyasu – from the late Heian period, attributed to the early Mito daimyō Tokugawa Yorifusa’s donation; overall length 77.5 cm; designated on March 24, Showa 36.<ref>[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/ken/kougei/4-34/4-34.html Tachi (inscribed “Kageyasu”)] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education)</ref>
** One pair of “Kusabana Sōchō Enkyo” (a circular mirror decorated with twin birds and floral motifs) – from the Muromachi period; although this item was reportedly stolen in 1970, it was designated on February 24, Showa 40.<ref>[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/ken/kougei/4-63/4-63.html Kusabana Sōchō Enkyo] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education)</ref>
** One eleven-faced Kannon statue (depicting the true form of the bodhisattva) – from the early Kamakura period; although it too was reportedly stolen in 1970, it was designated on February 24, Showa 40.<ref>[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/ken/kougei/4-64/4-64.html Eleven-faced Kannon Statue] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education)</ref>
** Eighteen volumes of Kashima Jingu documents (ancient texts) – ranging from a letter by Minamoto no Yoritomo dated Genryaku 2 (1185 AD) up to documents from the Ministry of Divinities in Meiji 4 (1871 AD), comprising approximately 250 items in scroll form, compiled into 18 volumes; designated on November 10, Heisei 22.<ref>[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/ken/komon/6-6/6-6.html Kashima Jingu Documents] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education)</ref>
* Natural Monuments:
** The Kashima Jingu Forest – designated on August 23, Showa 38.<ref name="Forest">[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/ken/tennen/14-28/14-28.html Kashima Jingu Forest] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education)</ref>

== Related Matters ==
=== Kashima District Government Office Ruins ===
[[File:Kashimaguuke-ato -3.JPG|thumb]]
The former Kashima District (formerly known as Kashima-gun, also called Kashima or Kashima-gun of Hitachi) was established according to the ''Hitachi Fudoki''<ref group="Primary Source" name="Fudoki">{{ill|Hitachi Fudoki|ja|常陸国風土記|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hitachi Fudoki|1=Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11481687}}</ref> as a divine district formed from portions of the territories of the maritime state and the inland state, and its administrative center is presumed to have been located near the shrine.<ref>{{sfn|Kashima District (Kadokawa)|1983}}</ref> Although no remains of an ancient district office have been found, its proximity to the shrine is inferred.<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu (Deities)|1984}}</ref>

New district office ruins dating from the 8th to early 10th centuries have been discovered about 1.5 km south of the shrine in Miyachu, Kashima City at the “Kanomuka Site” ({{Coord|35|57|19.29|N|140|38|01.67|E|region:JP-08_type:landmark|name=Kashima District Ruler Ruins (Kanomuka Site)}}). This complex – comprising remnants of a district government enclosure, administrative buildings, and a Shōsōin-style structure – corresponds with the description in the ''Hitachi Fudoki'' which states that “the district office is situated to the south of that shrine.” The site is designated as a National Historic Site as an annex of the Kashima Jingu grounds.<ref name="Kanomuka">[http://www.bunkajoho.pref.ibaraki.jp/fudoki/visit/04/index.html Kashima Jingu Grounds with the Kashima District Ruins “Kanomuka Site” (神野向遺跡)] – Visit the Hitachi Fudoki – 1300th Anniversary of the Hitachi Fudoki (Ibaraki Prefecture Lifestyle Culture Information Network)</ref><ref name="Historic Site"/>

Kashima Jingu’s divine progeny – that is, its branch shrines (often identified as its “descendant deities”) – were established throughout the former Hitachi region as Kashima’s power spread eastward along the coast. According to the ''Hitachi Fudoki''<ref group="Primary Source" name="Yukue">See the “Yukue-gun” section of the Hitachi Fudoki.</ref>, by the time of the 8th century there were already auxiliary shrines in the former 【Yukue District】 (now in Fukushima), and later the ''Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku'' (in the 8th year of the Zhenguan era, 866 AD)<ref group="Primary Source" name="Zhenguan8">''Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku'', Zhenguan 8, January 20 (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}).</ref> records that there were 38 such branch shrines in Mutsu Province.<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Mikuei Shrines (National History)|1983}}</ref> Their distribution – for example, 1 in Kikuta District, 11 in Iwaki District, 2 in Hyōba District, 1 in Yukue District (Fukushima), 7 in Uta District, 1 in Igu District, 2 in Saidori District, 3 in Miyagi District, 1 in Kurokawa District, 3 in Iroma District, 1 in Shidah District, 4 in Oda District, and 1 in Oshika District – attests to the spread of Kashima’s influence. In addition, the branch shrines of Kasuga Jingu, which bear the name “Ihahinoshi” (or “Iwai-nushi, Sai-nushi”) as an alternative name, are enshrined farther inland than those of Kashima, leading some scholars to suggest that initially Kashima was oriented toward the open sea (the territory of the Emishi) while Kasuga was oriented toward the inner sea (the {{ill|Katori Sea|en|Katori Sea|qid=Q11667182|lt=Kasatori-kai|1=Katori Sea}}), with their roles later becoming reversed.<ref>{{sfn|Kasuga Jingu (Deities)|1984}}</ref>

Additional evidence for Kashima’s expansion comes from the fact that many shrines enshrining Kashima’s deity were established nationwide as the Yamato regime advanced along the coast.<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu (Shikinaisha)|1976}}</ref>
=== Kashima’s “Seven Mysteries” ===
Kashima Jingu is also famed for its “Seven Mysteries,” a list of phenomena associated with the shrine that include:
* The sacred “kanameishi” (keystone)
* The depth of the water in the Mitarai Pond
* “Munamugawa” – a river outside the shrine whose source mysteriously disappears in the high lands of the heavens
* The abundance (or scarcity) of wisteria flowers on the three peaks of Mikasa Mountain – said to portend a bountiful or poor harvest, respectively
* The sound of the sea (uranari) on the Kashima Nada – when the waves’ sound is heard toward the north (near the Okugū), it forecasts clear weather; if heard to the south, rain is expected
* The “Neagari Pine” – a pine tree within the shrine grounds which, even after repeated pruning, always regenerates without withering
* “Pine Chopsticks” – chopsticks made from the shrine’s pine that are said never to exude oil

=== Kashima’s “Seven Mysteries” ===
The seven mysterious phenomena of Kashima Jingu are as follows:<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu (Shikinaisha)|1982}}</ref>
* The kanameishi (sacred keystone)
* The inexplicable depth of the Mitarai Pond’s water
* Munamugawa – a river outside the shrine where water, believed to have sprung from Takamagahara, vanishes without trace
* The flowering of wisteria on Mikasa Mountain – abundant blooms signal a bountiful harvest, while few blooms portend a poor yield
* The “sea cry” of Kashima Nada – near the Okugū, if the sound of the waves projects northward, clear weather is forecast; if southward, rain is expected
* The “Reneagari Pine” – a pine that, despite repeated felling, always sprouts anew
* The “Pine Chopsticks” – chopsticks crafted from the shrine’s pine that are said never to release oil

=== Other Related Items ===
; {{Anchor|Kashima Jingu-dera}} Kashima Jingu-dera  
: “Kashima Jingu-dera.” This was once a temple attached to Kashima Jingu.<br />According to official documents dated to the 3rd year of {{ill|Kashō|en|Kashō|qid=Q1373157|lt=Kashō|1=Kashō}} (850 AD)<ref group="Primary Source">Excerpt from ''Ruiju Sandai Kakuden'' Part 2, August 5, 850 AD (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}).</ref> and to the 3rd year of {{ill|Ten'an|ja|天安|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ten'an|1=Cheonan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q3577288}} (859 AD)<ref group="Primary Source">Excerpt from ''Ruiju Sandai Kakuden'' Part 3, February 16, 859 AD (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}).</ref>, it was founded by Kashima District governor {{ill|Nakatomi Tsuchitoku|ja|中臣連千徳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakatomi Tsuchitoku|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=DELETED_QID|dd=Q135491605}}, the former head priest {{ill|Nakatomi Ōsō|ja|中臣鹿島連大宗|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakatomi Ōsō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|qid=DELETED_QID|dd=Q135491607}} (taisō), and the monk {{ill|Mankai|ja|万巻|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mankai|1=Mangan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11353818}}, during the Tenpyō era (749–757 AD); it was later listed among the temples with fixed stipends (teigaku-dera) in the 4th year of the Shōwa era (837 AD) and played an important role as a branch temple during the Nanboku-chō period.<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu-dera (National History)|1983}}</ref>
; Kashima-dachi
: “Kashima-dachi” means “departure” or “embarkation” and is said to have originated from Kashima Jingu. One explanation is that, following Kashima Jingu’s role in subjugating the land, soldiers and warriors prayed at the shrine for a safe departure.<ref name="Kashima-dachi">[https://kotobank.jp/word/%E9%B9%BF%E5%B3%B6%E7%AB%8B%E3%81%A1-462178 {{ill|Kotobank: Kashima-dachi|ja|鹿島立ち|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotobank: Kashima-dachi|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}]</ref> In connection with this, a poem by unknown authors in the ''Manyōshū'' is also well known.<ref group="Primary Source">{{sfn|Kashima Jingu (Shikinaisha)|1982}}</ref>
: {{Cquote|{{Small|In the seventh year of the Taimyo era, on a cold February day, as the rain fell, I prayed to Kashima’s deity – and thus I set forth to join the imperial army.|20px}}}}
: Also, when Tokugawa Mitsukuni of Mito Domain visited Kashima Jingu in the first year of {{ill|Kōgen|en|Kōgen|qid=Q1194242|lt=Kōgen|1=Kōgen}} (1256 AD), he referred to the kanameishi as “the Stone Seat” (Ishimimashi) and composed a poem:<br />{{Cquote|“I wonder if I shall find it today, the stone seat hidden deep within the mountain’s recesses, where the thousand swords have been shattered…”|20px}}<ref>{{sfn|Kashima Jingu Chronicle|2004|p=19}}</ref>
